study_identification.title: Patterns of connectome variability in autism across five functional activation tasks: findings from the LEAP project

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize heterogeneity in autism by identifying patterns of neural diversity as reflected in BOLD fMRI in the way individuals with autism engage with a varied array of cognitive tasks, using a novel task potency approach combined with normative modeling to map individual-level atypicality.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FSL; MCFLIRT (motion correction); global 4D mean intensity normalization; 6 mm FWHM smoothing; ICA-AROMA (motion artifact removal); WM/CSF regression; 0.01 Hz high-pass filter; FLIRT (BBR to T1); FNIRT (nonlinear to MNI152); inverse transform to native space; ComBat (site harmonization)
preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The preprocessing section provides detailed step-by-step description of the FSL-based pipeline including motion correction, normalization, smoothing, ICA-AROMA, nuisance regression, high-pass filtering, registration steps, and ComBat harmonization.
preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Preprocessing of both the resting state- and task-fMRI data was performed with tools from FSL [35]. The first five volumes for each acquisition were removed to allow for equilibration of the magnetization. To correct for head movement, we performed volume realignment to the middle volume using MCFLIRT. Next, global 4D mean intensity normalization and smoothing with a 6 mm FWHM kernel were applied. ICA-AROMA was used to identify and remove secondary motion-related artifacts [36, 37]. Next, signal from white matter and cerebrospinal fluid was regressed out and we applied a 0.01 Hz high-pass filter. For each participant, we registered acquisitions to their respective high-resolution T1 anatomical images by means of the Boundary-Based Registration tool from FSL-FLIRT [24]. The high-resolution T1 image belonging to each participant was registered to MNI152 space with FLIRT 12-degrees of freedom linear registration, and further refined using FNIRT nonlinear registration [38]. We used the inverse of these transformations to take a brain atlas to the native space of each participant, where all further analyses were performed. ComBat was used to clean the data for linear site effects [39].

response_variable.answer: Task potency connectivity edges (partial correlation values between 168 ICP atlas regions, task minus rest FC matrices); per-edge Z-scores of atypicality
response_variable.reason: The response variable is clearly described: task potency values, which are connectivity modulations away from resting state baseline. Specifically, regularized partial correlations (Fisher-Z transformed) are computed for 168×168 region pairs, then task minus rest is calculated to derive task potency. These edge values are then modeled to produce Z-scores.
response_variable.supporting_text: For each participant, we calculated the regularized covariance [41] between the average BOLD time series extracted from each brain region pair. We then estimated partial correlations from the covariance matrix and consecutively applied the Fisher-Z transformation. This provided for each participant a connectivity matrix of size 168 × 168—one resting state matrix and one task-fMRI matrix per task. ... In order to produce individual matrices of connectivity modulations induced by the task, i.e., task potency, we subtracted each participant's resting state connectivity matrix from that participant's task connectivity matrix. ... A normative model of potency edge values was built ... Task potency values were thereby transformed to Z-scores quantifying the atypicality per edge

deviation_metric.answer: Per-edge Z-scores from normative model; percentage of connectome exceeding |z| ≥ 2.571 threshold (nominally top/bottom 1% extreme values); independent t-tests comparing ASD vs TD percentages (FDR-corrected across tasks); Cohen's D effect sizes
deviation_metric.reason: The deviation metric is clearly described: task potency edge values are transformed to Z-scores via normative modeling. A threshold of |z| ≥ 2.571 is applied to identify the 1% most extreme edges. The percentage of edges exceeding this threshold is calculated per individual and compared between groups using independent t-tests with FDR correction and Cohen's D.
deviation_metric.supporting_text: Task potency values were thereby transformed to Z-scores quantifying the atypicality per edge of each individual's task potency matrix elements given the normative reference. This was done separately in each task. ... Percentage of connectome deemed atypical was identified by thresholding the Z-scores at z = | ± 2.571|, nominally describing the 1% most extreme positive and negative values. The number of edges passing this threshold for each individual was then expressed as a percentage of the total amount of edges. Independent t tests were performed on the percentages to assess case-control differences in the tasks. All p values were FDR corrected for multiple comparisons across tasks. Cohen's D was calculated for an effect size estimate in each task.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Case-control group differences assessed via independent t-tests on percentage of atypical edges (FDR-corrected across tasks) with Cohen's D effect sizes. Robust out-of-sample canonical correlation analysis (CCA) with 1000-fold tenfold cross-validation splits related brain atypicality patterns (top 10 PCA components of edgewise Z-scores) to behavioral measures (SRS, RBS, SSP, ADHD hyperactivity/impulsivity, ADHD inattentiveness, Vineland, IQ). CCA significance assessed via permutation testing (within-site subject permutation). Cross-task similarity of atypicality patterns evaluated via Pearson correlation matrices of mean edgewise atypicality, compared between ASD and TD groups using Wilcoxon signed rank test.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: ASD showed greater global functional connectivity atypicality than TD across all five tasks (all p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.19-0.61), with significantly increased cross-task similarity in deviation patterns compared to TD (p<0.002). Robust brain-behavior CCA identified significant covariation between FC atypicality and autism-related behaviors across all tasks.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Deviation from normative ranges of global functional connectivity was significantly greater for ASD compared to TD in each task: Flanker (Cohen's d=0.61, p<0.01), Hariri (d=0.34, p<0.01), Theory of Mind (d=0.36, p<0.01), Monetary reward (d=0.19, p<0.01), Social reward (d=0.19, p<0.01). Cross-task Pearson correlations of edgewise atypicality patterns were consistently higher in ASD (mean r=0.43) than TD (mean r=0.07), with significant group difference (Wilcoxon p<0.002). Spatial patterns of atypicality originated primarily from prefrontal cortex, default mode network, speech networks, and auditory networks across tasks. CCA revealed significant and robust brain-behavior covariation in all tasks (loadings stability >0.99 under tenfold CV), with behavioral loadings in the direction of greater impairment across SRS, RBS, SSP, ADHD symptoms, and Vineland. IQ showed involvement in Hariri and Flanker tasks but minimal loading in reward and ToM tasks. Results suggest individuals with ASD engage with tasks in a globally atypical way, but the spatial pattern of atypicality shows clear similarity across cognitive domains.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Functional connectivity exhibits test-retest variability driven by factors such as participant traits, time of day, caffeine, medication, and task magnitude. While task potency uses each individual as their own baseline (task minus rest from same scan session) to control for some sources of variability, remaining variability may affect FC fingerprints. Brain plots should not be regarded as equivalent to activation maps; highlighted areas indicate involvement through up- or downregulation of coupling with other areas, not isolated activation. Tasks were chosen for autism relevance but other forms of cognitive engagement may be needed for complete cross-task perspective. Though individual atypicality metrics are used, normative range estimation treats TD as a single group, potentially masking ASD subgroups embedded in the TD range.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Introduces task potency approach (task minus rest connectivity) with mixture Gaussian-gamma model normalization for FC edge values. Normative modeling with age/sex adjustment implemented in nispat (Python). ComBat harmonization for site effects. Robust out-of-sample CCA (1000 splits of tenfold CV, within-site permutation testing) linking deviations to behavior. ICP parcellation (168 regions, 11 networks). Regularized covariance for partial correlations. Fisher-Z transformation. Cross-task similarity analysis revealing higher similarity in ASD than TD. Neurosynth decoder used to interpret spatial patterns of atypicality.

general_notes.general_notes: Five task-fMRI paradigms: (1) Hariri emotion processing (select matching emotional face), (2) Flanker/Go-NoGo (arrow direction with congruent/incongruent flankers), (3) Social reward anticipation (fast button press rewarded with happy face), (4) Nonsocial/monetary reward anticipation (fast button press rewarded with monetary stimulus), (5) Animated shapes Theory of Mind (categorize triangle videos as random, goal-directed, or mentalizing). Multi-echo EPI sequence for rs-fMRI (TR=2300ms, TEs=12/31/48ms, 200-265 volumes depending on site). MPRAGE for T1 (TR=2300ms, TE=2.93ms, 1.1×1.1×1.2mm voxels). Six European sites: KCL, RUNMC, UMCU, ARC/UCAM, CIMH (KI excluded for low N). First 5 volumes removed. Task-specific sample sizes vary (see supplementary tables S1-S5). Behavioral measures: SRS (social responsiveness), RBS (repetitive behaviors), SSP (sensory profile), ADHD rating scale components, Vineland adaptive functioning, WASI-II IQ. Missing behavioral data imputed with random forest regression. Novel finding: cross-task similarity of atypicality patterns significantly higher in ASD than TD, supporting common deficit theories. Full statistical values for Figure 1 provided in supplementary Table T1. Supplementary figures show: analytical pipeline (S1), difference between normative atypicality and CCA loadings (S2), FD vs atypicality regressions for all tasks (S3A-E), with/without ComBat site correction comparison (S4A-E).
